christianity and family law
The Western tradition has always cherished the family as an essential foundation
of a just and orderly society, and thus accorded it special legal and religious
protection.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Christianity embraced this teaching from the start, and many of the basics of Western family law were shaped by Christian theologies of nature, sacrament, and covenant.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Each of these introductions offers fresh scholarship into historical, doc- trinal, and comparative perspectives on Christian sources and dimensions of familiar legal topics.
text_raw:
Each of these introductions offers fresh scholarship into historical, doc-
trinal, and comparative perspectives on Christian sources and dimensions of
familiar legal topics.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Although the chapters are written by leading experts, they are intended for nonspecialists in colleges and in graduate and professional schools, as well as for clergy, interested laity, and scholars from other ﬁelds.
text_raw:
Although the chapters are written by leading experts, they
are intended for nonspecialists in colleges and in graduate and professional
schools, as well as for clergy, interested laity, and scholars from other ﬁelds.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The aim is to illuminate what Christianity has contributed and continues to offer to the world of law, particularly in the West.
text_raw:
The aim is to illuminate what Christianity has contributed and continues to
offer to the world of law, particularly in the West.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The volume in hand analyzes Christian inﬂuences on Western family law.
text_raw: The volume in hand analyzes Christian inﬂuences on Western family law.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: The main legal topics include the formation, maintenance, and dissolution of marriage; relations between husbands and wives, parents and children, and siblings and kinsmen within and beyond the household; and important dimensions of human sexuality and intimacy.
text_raw:
The main legal topics include the formation, maintenance, and dissolution of
marriage; relations between husbands and wives, parents and children, and
siblings and kinsmen within and beyond the household; and important
dimensions of human sexuality and intimacy.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: This volume also touches more lightly on related legal topics of marital property and inheritance; the structure of the household and its role in public and private life; and house- hold order, including women’s rights, children’s rights, and master–servant relations.
text_raw:
This volume also touches
more lightly on related legal topics of marital property and inheritance; the
structure of the household and its role in public and private life; and house-
hold order, including women’s rights, children’s rights, and master–servant
relations.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Christian theology and the church’s canon law had a decisive inﬂuence on these topics of Western family law for nearly two millennia. xix Published online by Cambridge University Press
text_raw:
Christian theology and the church’s canon law had a decisive
inﬂuence on these topics of Western family law for nearly two millennia.
xix
Published online by Cambridge University Press

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: From the fourth to the nineteenth centuries, church and state cooperated in the governance of the marital family, and an established Christian culture shaped sexual ethics.
text_raw:
From the fourth to the nineteenth centuries, church and state cooperated in
the governance of the marital family, and an established Christian culture
shaped sexual ethics.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Today the modern secular state has assumed jurisdiction over most family law questions, and Western culture has disestablished Christianity and liberalized sex, marriage, and family norms.
text_raw:
Today the modern secular state has assumed jurisdiction
over most family law questions, and Western culture has disestablished
Christianity and liberalized sex, marriage, and family norms.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: Nonetheless, many churches in and beyond the West continue to maintain internal laws and procedures to govern the family lives of their members, and Christian leaders continue to inﬂuence family law policies and advocate for their reform.
text_raw:
Nonetheless,
many churches in and beyond the West continue to maintain internal laws
and procedures to govern the family lives of their members, and Christian
leaders continue to inﬂuence family law policies and advocate for their
reform.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: To tell this complex story in a single volume, we focus on twenty-eight titans who helped to shape the theory and law of sex, marriage, and family life in the West from biblical times until today.
text_raw:
To tell this complex story in a single volume, we focus on twenty-eight titans
who helped to shape the theory and law of sex, marriage, and family life in the
West from biblical times until today.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: We have selected illustrative ﬁgures whose contributions to this tradition were both distinct and enduring.
text_raw:
We have selected illustrative ﬁgures
whose contributions to this tradition were both distinct and enduring.

chapter_title: Frontmatter
text: We have sought to balance Catholics, Protestants, and a few Orthodox ﬁgures who had inﬂuence in the West, and have placed leading popes, emperors, and kings alongside inﬂuential jurists, theologians, and philosophers.
text_raw:
We have sought to balance Catholics, Protestants, and a few Orthodox ﬁgures
who had inﬂuence in the West, and have placed leading popes, emperors, and
kings alongside inﬂuential jurists, theologians, and philosophers.

gradually given way to modern liberalism and post-Christian teachings.

text: But Augustine’s writings are also signiﬁcant because they addressed topics that were of pressing concern to his Christian contemporaries: in ear ly treatises against the Manichaeans he argued against his former coreligionists for the goodness of marriage; in response to debates about marriage and celibacy, he offered a balanced account of the good features of marriag e, while insisting on the superior status of celibacy; in his later writings against the Pelagians, he noted in the vagaries of sexual desire a privileged symptom of the “original sin.” All of these contexts shaped the development of the distinctive ideas that have come to be known as “Augustinian.” The course of Augustine’s early life is well known because of his own narrative in the Confessions , but some salient features should be mentioned here.

chapter_title: Chapter 5), have proved welcome additions to modern Western Christian
text: As David Ford writes, “St John Chrysostom ﬁlls the pattern of male headship/superiority with profoundly Christian content, enriching it to a far greater degree than it was understood and practiced at the time by his surrounding non-Christian society.” 28 A stunning illustration of this occurs at the start of Chrysostom’s homily on Ephesians 5:22–33, where he brilliantly juxtaposes Genesis 1:27 and Galatians 32:28, so that there can be little doubt about his high, even sacramental understanding of being married “in the Lord.” This homily excludes a servile subordination of the wife to her husband, but indicates, rather, a unity of two human beings as a single nuptial and ecclesial “body,” which transcends the artiﬁcial gender differences and ideologies that human beings, not God, have invented.

BIOGRAPHICAL INTRODUCTION
Theodoros Balsamon ﬂourished near the end of the twelfth century CE,
during the reign of Emperor Manuel Komnenos and the incumbency of
Balsamon’s patron, Constantinopolitan Patriarch Michael Anchialos.

text_raw:
BALSAMON’S CONTRIBUTIONS TO THE ORTHODOX CANON
LAW OF THE FAMILY
While serving as nomophylax, around the year 1170, Balsamon was asked by
Patriarch Michael to publish a signiﬁcant review of church law attributed to the
ninth-century Patriarch Photios, called the Exegesis of the Nomokanon in 14
Titles.1 This was an authoritative listing of the key church canons and parallel
civil norms.

Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences, was a prominent participant in

From 1515 to 1545, Luther issued a torrent of writings that ﬁll nearly one
hundred thick folio volumes.2 These included a famous German translation of
the Bible; sundry biblical commentaries and sermons; church liturgies and
songs; church laws, catechisms, and confessional tracts; polemical writings
and table talks; formal consilia and private letters; various pamphlets and two
dozen substantial tracts on legal, political, economic, and social reforms.

text: THE GOODS AND GIFTS OF MARRIAGE AND FAMILY LIFE Luther was utterly conventional in teaching that marriage was created by God as a “two-in-one-ﬂesh” union between a man and a woman with the freedom, ﬁtness, and capacity to marry each other.
text_raw:
THE GOODS AND GIFTS OF MARRIAGE AND FAMILY LIFE
Luther was utterly conventional in teaching that marriage was created by God
as a “two-in-one-ﬂesh” union between a man and a woman with the freedom,
ﬁtness, and capacity to marry each other.

23
MARRIAGE IS NOT A SACRAMENT, BUT A SOCIAL ESTATE
While marriage was a creation and gift of God for the couple and their
children, it remained a social institution of the earthly kingdom, not a sacra-
ment of the heavenly kingdom.

chapter_title: Chapter 20 by Russell Hittinger on Pope Leo XIII.

BIOGRAPHICAL INTRODUCTION
John Calvin ( 1509–64) was the French humanistically trained lawyer and
later Protestant theologian and minister who spearheaded the religious
reformation of the Swiss city of Geneva between 1536 and 1564 (apart from
an interlude in Strasbourg from 1538 to 1541).

MARRIAGE
The reorganization of the church and civil life occasioned by Geneva’s newly
won independence and adoption of Reformed religion resulted in the devel-
opment of policies toward marriage starting in the 1540s.

AND AFFINITY
Matrimony had been designated as the seventh sacrament in the twelfth
century; unlike the other sacraments, however, it had not been instituted by
Christ during his ministry on earth, but rather by God in the Garden of Eden.2
Therefore the laws laid down in the Old Testament regarding who could and
could not marry were thought to remain in force.

chapter_title: chapter 1.
text: In the opening chapters of the Rights of Woman , Wollstonecraft deﬁned rights as “the privilege of moral beings.” Moral beings are human beings, designed by God to achieve “pre-eminence over the brute creation” through the exercise of “reason” to acquire “virtue” and “k nowledge.” She argued that women might “procure” rights through the “exercise of reason.” By using reason to gauge moral action toward othe rs, women would “obtain the sober pleasures that arise from equality.” She insisted that such “sober plea- sures” were secondary to the primary reason for women’s understanding of themselves as rights-bearing subje cts: women’s “ﬁrst duty is to them- selves as rational creatures.” The rights of women were therefore deriva- tive of their duties, especially the duty to develop their moral and intellectual potential as rational creatures of God.

Wollstonecraft’s theory of women’s human rights, as grounded on her
Christian metaphysics and ethics, has strong implications for the egalitarian
reform of family law.

text: The introduction to the document observes, “the Church has always had the duty of scrutinizing the signs of the times and of interpreting them in the light of the Gospel.” 1 One of the key domains of the times is marriage and the family, addressed in the second half of the document as one of ﬁve “problems of special urgency.” 2 This part of Gaudium et Spes, titled “Fostering the nobility [or dignity] of marriage and the family,” begins by noting that families are challenged by divorce, polygamy, sexual promiscuity, the rise of overt hedonism, and “illicit practices against human generation.”3 The health of society depends on the health of families, and the health of families depends on the health of marriages, but both marriage and family are threatened by unjust and degrading economic, social, and political conditions.

chapter_title: chapter 1.
text: As an intimate union of husband and wife into one ﬂesh, marriage is fundamentally a matter of love, which, “merging the human with the divine, leads the spouses to a free and mutual gift of themselves, a gift providing itself by gentle affection and by deed[;] such love pervades the whole of their lives: indeed by its busy generosity it grows better and grows greater.” 5 Such love would and should “never be profaned by adultery or divorce.” 6 This attractive vision of marriage was accepted despite the initial resistance of a number of bishops, who during the document’s drafting objected that the stress on marital love hits an emotional note that would weaken acknowl- edgment of the irrevocable (indissoluble) character of the sacrament.

text: Christian Green BIOGRAPHICAL INTRODUCTION Jean Bethke Elshtain (1941–2013) was neither a lawyer nor a scholar of law, but rather a singularly ﬂuid and adept scholar of political theory and religious ethics.
text_raw:
Christian Green
BIOGRAPHICAL INTRODUCTION
Jean Bethke Elshtain (1941–2013) was neither a lawyer nor a scholar of law, but
rather a singularly ﬂuid and adept scholar of political theory and religious
ethics.

chapter_title: chapter 1.
text: Her professional and scholarly career at Brandeis, Vanderbilt, and the University of Chicago began with the topics of feminism and the family and eventually expanded to include Christian just war theory, Augustinian poli- tical theology, theories of sovereignty of states and selves, and more.
text_raw:
Her professional and scholarly career at Brandeis, Vanderbilt, and the
University of Chicago began with the topics of feminism and the family and
eventually expanded to include Christian just war theory, Augustinian poli-
tical theology, theories of sovereignty of states and selves, and more.

chapter_title: chapter 1.
text: In essay upon essay – the genre in which her erudition and expressive powers shone especially brightly – she covered a comprehensive range of concerns at the intersection of politics, religion, ethics, and law on matters of domestic, national, and international importance.

especially brightly – she covered a comprehensive range of concerns at the

national, and international importance.

text: Her personal religious journey led this granddaughter of Russian-German immigrants to America from her original Lutheranism to reception into the Roman Catholic Church in the years before her death in 2013.

chapter_title: chapter 1.
text: Indeed, Elshtain argued with characteristically robust rhetoric, “For feminists to discover in the state the new ‘Mr. Right,’ and to wed themselves thereby, for better or for worse, to a public identity inseparable from the exigencies of state power and policy would be a mistake.” 3 In the face of this then- dominant androgynous and statist version of feminism, Elshtain declared her project to “reclaim for women a social identity that locates them very much in and of the wider world but positions them against overweening state power and public identity deﬁned in its terms.” In other words, as she put it, “My aim is to deﬁne and to defend a female identity and a feminist perspective that enables contemporary women to see themselves as the daughters of Antigone.” 4 For Elshtain, the story of Antigone provided an entre ´ e into examining the relationships among men, women, families, and the state in her landmark ﬁrst book, Public Man, Private Woman.

text: Liberal theorists “recast distinctions between public and private in order to take the family out of the politics and politics out of the family.”18 For women, “the effect of these splits was to further privatize the private world and to reduce the language of women to that of cloying sentiment as the private world was cut off even further from public discourse.” 19 Even though there was risk in this sort of hyper-privatization of the family, public solutions, in Elshtain’s view, are not always a panacea. “Public grants of parity to women have gone hand in glove within liberalism ... with extraordinary disparity in the distribution of goods and services and in the concrete allocation of economic and social power.”20 Particularly troubling for Elshtain in the social contractarian theories of Hobbes, Locke, and other early liberal theorists was the hypertrophy of the contractual ideal, especially in the family.
